title: File descriptors and open files
description: Learn how Linux uses file descriptors to manage files, sockets, and pipes in production.

data.text: A file descriptor is a number that the Linux kernel uses to keep track of an open file or resource. Every time a process opens a file, creates a network connection, or starts a pipe, the kernel gives it a file descriptor. These numbers are not just for regular files: they also represent sockets, pipes, and devices.

If your application suddenly cannot start new connections or says too many files are open, the problem is almost always file descriptors. Understanding how to inspect and manage them is a core Linux troubleshooting skill.

When a process starts, it automatically gets three file descriptors: stdin (0), stdout (1), and stderr (2). Every additional open file, socket, or pipe gets the next available number. The maximum number of file descriptors a process can have is controlled by the soft limit and hard limit, which you can see with ulimit.

data.code:
ulimit -n          # show current soft limit
ulimit -Hn         # show hard limit
cat /proc/1234/limits  # show limits for PID 1234

data.text: The lsof command lists open files for a process or the entire system. It shows which files, sockets, and pipes are open, and which process is using them. This is invaluable when a process will not shut down cleanly or when you need to know why a file cannot be deleted.

data.code:
lsof -p 1234                # files opened by PID 1234
lsof -i :8080                 # who is using port 8080
lsof +L1                      # deleted files still held open

data.title: The +L1 trick
data.text: A file that is deleted but still held open by a process will not free disk space until the process closes it. Use lsof +L1 to find these files. Restarting the process usually releases them.

items: Too many open files: increase the limit with ulimit -n or update /etc/security/limits.conf
Leaked descriptors: a process that opens files without closing them eventually runs out of descriptors
Cannot delete a file: a running process still has it open; stop the process or restart it
Socket exhaustion: each network connection uses a file descriptor; a busy server can exhaust the limit

data.text: The /proc filesystem provides a view into every process. The /proc/[pid]/fd directory contains symbolic links to all open file descriptors. Reading this directory gives you a direct snapshot of what a process has open, without needing lsof.

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: File descriptors are numbers representing open files, sockets, and pipes
Every process starts with stdin, stdout, and stderr (0, 1, 2)
Use lsof to see which files a process has open
Too many open files causes failures; increase ulimit -n when needed
Deleted files still held open by processes waste disk space until the process closes them
